name: Coursera, Inc.

profile.description: Coursera is the world's largest online learning platform following its May 2026 all-stock merger with Udemy, offering over 12,000 courses, professional certificates, and degree programs from 325+ university and industry partners to consumers, enterprises, and government customers globally. The company is a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation and certified B Corp with approximately 1,307 employees. Q2 FY2026 revenue reached $299M (+60% YoY including Udemy) with full-year guidance raised to $1.22-$1.245B, while organic Q1 growth was 9.1% to $195.7M [1][2].

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (2/3): The all-stock merger with Udemy (closed May 2026) is a significant strategic move that created the dominant global online learning platform, consolidating two of the top three players and adding enterprise training capabilities to Coursera's academic strength [2]. This acquisition opened substantial new revenue streams through Udemy's B2B corporate training business. AI Deployment (1/2): Coursera has deployed AI features including the Coursera Coach AI tutor and AI-powered content creation tools, and the platform now hosts 1,100+ generative AI courses representing a 44% YoY increase [3]. However, no specific revenue or cost savings from AI features have been quantified. Market Share (2/2): Post-Udemy merger, Coursera is the dominant online learning platform globally with the largest catalog (12,000+ courses), the broadest university partnership network (325+ institutions), and an expanded enterprise offering — a clear category leader [2]. Product Pipeline (1/2): Post-merger integration roadmap includes unified enterprise platform and expanded degree offerings, but specific product launch timelines are vague beyond general 'platform innovation' language. R&D Intensity (0/1): No specific R&D spending data available as a percentage of revenue to compare against education technology peers.

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): Coursera's mission — to provide universal access to world-class learning — is specific, thoughtful, and genuinely purposeful, institutionalized through its legal structure as a Public Benefit Corporation and certified B Corp [4]. Co-founder Andrew Ng (who chairs the board) built the company explicitly to democratize education from top universities, and strategic decisions (free audit access, government partnerships for workforce development) trace back to this purpose. Falls short of a 4 because the new CEO's Amazon-style cultural transformation and the Udemy merger prioritize growth over mission purity. Community Impact (1/2): As a PBC/B Corp, Coursera provides free content access programs and government workforce development partnerships, though specific dollar amounts or measurable community impact are not widely reported [4]. Employee Retention (0/2): New CEO Greg Hart (joined February 2025 from Amazon) has implemented cultural realignment with 'leadership mindsets' modeled on Amazon principles, which may create retention uncertainty during a major transition [3]. No specific turnover or tenure data available. Insider Buying (0/2): No evidence of meaningful net insider buying in the last 12 months.

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Growth stock, excluding Forward PEG (not reported by yfinance due to the company's transition from losses to profitability). D/E of 0.8% is exceptionally low, scoring 1.0 — the company holds $982M in cash against just $9.7M in debt, providing a fortress balance sheet [1]. Revenue growth of 59.6% YoY scores 1.0, though this is inflated by the Udemy merger (organic Q1 growth was 9.1%) [1][2]. Estimated 5-year revenue CAGR of ~16% (from ~$415M in 2021 to ~$885M TTM pre-merger) scores 1.0 at 2x weight. Forward P/E of 6.0 scores 1.0, reflecting extremely low valuation relative to growth — the stock trades at just $4.94 near its 52-week low of $4.53 [1]. ROE of -15.2% scores 0.0 at 2x weight, reflecting ongoing GAAP losses. Profit margin of -15.4% scores 0.0, though non-GAAP gross margin improved to 62% in Q2 [2]. Daily dollar volume of $30.9M provides adequate liquidity.

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (4/9): Coursera faces meaningful AI disruption risk across multiple business lines. AI tutoring tools (ChatGPT, Google's LearnLM, Khan Academy's Khanmigo) can replicate much of the personalized instruction that individual online courses provide, potentially reducing the value proposition of pre-recorded lecture content [3]. The company's non-degree courses and skills-based certificates — which drive significant consumer and enterprise revenue — face substitution risk from AI-powered learning tools that can teach skills interactively and on-demand. The defensive moat rests on university partnerships for accredited degrees and certificates that AI cannot replicate (employers still value institutional credentials), and the enterprise platform's integration with corporate learning management systems creates switching costs. However, the pace of AI-driven learning innovation creates genuine uncertainty about whether Coursera's marketplace model will maintain its value as AI tutors become more capable. AI Opportunity (1/1): Coursera generates direct revenue from 1,100+ generative AI courses (44% YoY growth), and the Coursera Coach AI tutor enhances platform engagement [3]. AI skills training is one of the fastest-growing content categories on the platform.

infinite_game.summary: Coursera demonstrates a mixed infinite game orientation — a genuine Just Cause around democratizing education that is institutionalized in its B Corp structure, combined with recent leadership changes and a major acquisition that introduce uncertainty about whether purpose or growth will drive decisions. The Udemy merger consolidates market position but the Amazon-style cultural transformation under new CEO Greg Hart may prioritize operational efficiency over mission-driven innovation.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): Coursera's founding cause — universal access to world-class learning — is genuinely idealistic, inclusive, and bigger than any single product, institutionalized through the company's legal structure as a Public Benefit Corporation and B Corp [4]. Co-founder Andrew Ng's continued involvement as board chair provides cause continuity, and strategic decisions (free content access, government partnerships) trace to the mission. However, the cause has not been tested through major crisis or multi-decade consistency — the company is only 14 years old, and the CEO transition and Udemy merger introduce questions about whether growth strategy may drift from educational mission toward revenue optimization [3].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): The all-stock Udemy merger is a bold strategic bet to consolidate the online learning market, accepting near-term integration risk and GAAP losses (Q2 net loss of $80.4M) to build long-term market dominance [2]. CEO Greg Hart's willingness to implement Amazon-style cultural transformation at a mission-driven B Corp shows conviction, though it remains to be seen whether this courage serves the cause or merely imports corporate playbooks [3].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Coursera maintains a lean organization of 1,307 employees with a new CEO implementing 'leadership mindsets' and an 'AI Sparks' forum encouraging employee experimentation with automation [3]. The company's B Corp culture historically emphasized mission alignment, but the Amazon-style management approach under Greg Hart may create cultural tension. No specific evidence of exceptional trust or significant organizational instability.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): The Udemy merger represents meaningful strategic evolution — from a university-focused MOOC platform to a comprehensive enterprise and consumer learning ecosystem encompassing skills training, professional development, and degree programs [2]. This is a significant expansion of the business model, though incremental rather than transformative, as it consolidates an adjacent market rather than entering an entirely new one.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No evidence that Coursera's leadership frames competition through a lens of self-improvement. The Udemy acquisition suggests a strategy of eliminating a rival through consolidation rather than learning from its strengths. CEO Hart's Amazon background emphasizes market dominance rather than worthy rival appreciation.

investment_thesis: Coursera at $4.94 with a $1.4B market cap offers a deeply discounted entry into the world's largest online learning platform, trading at just 6x forward earnings and near its 52-week low of $4.53 despite the transformative Udemy merger creating a dominant market position [1][2]. The combined entity guides to $1.22-$1.245B in FY2026 revenue with a fortress balance sheet ($982M cash, $9.7M debt), while non-GAAP gross margin expanded to 62% in Q2, suggesting a path to sustained profitability as merger synergies are realized [2]. Secular tailwinds from AI-driven workforce reskilling, enterprise upskilling demand, and the global shift toward credentialed online education support long-term growth in a market where Coursera now holds the broadest partner network (325+ universities) and course catalog (12,000+ courses).
thesis_continued: The bear case centers on AI disruption risk and unproven merger execution. Coursera's core product — pre-recorded online courses — faces genuine substitution risk from AI tutoring tools (ChatGPT, Khanmigo, LearnLM) that can provide personalized, interactive instruction without the rigid structure of traditional MOOCs [3]. Organic revenue growth of just 9.1% in Q1 (before the Udemy acquisition inflated reported numbers to 60%) suggests the underlying business is decelerating from prior double-digit rates [1]. The GAAP net loss of $80.4M in Q2 and negative profit margin of -15.4% raise profitability questions, especially as the company digests a complex merger integration. CEO Greg Hart's Amazon-style cultural transformation at a B Corp introduces execution risk — the tension between growth-optimization management and mission-driven culture could result in talent attrition or strategic drift. At $4.94, the stock has lost 54% from its 52-week high of $10.77, reflecting market skepticism about whether the Udemy merger will unlock value or compound complexity [1].
key_catalysts: Udemy merger synergies — integration of Udemy's enterprise training platform with Coursera's university credentials network could unlock cross-selling opportunities, with full-year revenue guidance of $1.22-$1.245B implying significant combined scale [2]

AI-driven workforce reskilling demand — enterprises are accelerating upskilling investments as AI transforms job requirements, with Coursera's 1,100+ generative AI courses (up 44% YoY) positioned to capture this secular tailwind [3]

Path to GAAP profitability — forward P/E of 6.0x with non-GAAP gross margin expanding to 62% suggests the transition to sustained profitability could rerate the stock significantly from its current depressed valuation near 52-week lows [1][2]
key_risks: AI substitution risk to core product — pre-recorded online courses face growing competition from AI tutoring tools that provide personalized, interactive learning experiences without rigid course structures, threatening the value proposition of Coursera's marketplace model [3]

Organic growth deceleration — pre-merger Q1 revenue grew only 9.1% YoY, down from prior quarters of double-digit growth, suggesting the underlying business faces maturation headwinds masked by the Udemy acquisition [1]

Merger integration risk — combining Coursera and Udemy's platforms, cultures, and enterprise sales teams while a new CEO simultaneously implements Amazon-style cultural transformation creates multi-layered execution risk that could disrupt both businesses [2][3]
